title: Soil

learn.summary: Soil is a living system, not dirt: minerals, organic matter, air, water, and billions of organisms per handful. Most garden problems trace back to soil, and most soil problems are fixed the same way — add organic matter yearly. A $15-25 lab soil test from your state Extension service beats guessing every time.

do: Order a soil test kit from your state Cooperative Extension this week and pull samples from 4-6 spots at 6 inches deep

children.title: Soil Microbiome

learn.summary: A teaspoon of healthy soil holds more microbes than there are people on Earth — bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes — cycling nutrients into plant-available forms. Mycorrhizal fungi partner with roughly 80% of plant species, trading soil phosphorus for plant sugars. Feed this web with compost and mulch; tilling and bare soil starve it.

do: Do a worm count: dig one cubic foot of moist garden soil and count earthworms — 10 or more signals a healthy soil food web

children.title: Texture & Structure

learn.summary: Texture is your fixed sand-silt-clay ratio; structure is how those particles clump, and structure is what you can improve. Sandy soil drains fast and starves; clay holds nutrients but waterlogs and compacts. The fix for both extremes is identical: 2-3 inches of compost worked into the top layer every year.

do: Run the jar test: shake soil and water in a mason jar, let it settle 24 hours, and read your sand/silt/clay layers

children.title: pH & Testing

learn.summary: Most vegetables want pH 6.0-7.0; blueberries, azaleas, and potatoes prefer acidic 4.5-5.5. Outside a plant's range, nutrients lock up chemically no matter how much fertilizer you add. Raise pH with lime, lower it with elemental sulfur — both take months, so test in fall and amend only per lab recommendation.

do: When your soil test results arrive, write the pH and top two nutrient recommendations into your garden notebook and buy only what it prescribes

children.title: Amendments

learn.summary: Compost is the universal amendment; everything else is situational. Aged manure adds nitrogen but must be composted 6+ months (fresh manure burns roots and carries pathogens); leaf mold improves water retention; sand added to clay makes concrete, not loam — skip it. Target 5% organic matter on your soil test.

do: Spread a 2-inch layer of compost on one bed this week and fork it into the top 6 inches
